newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA moves to quell cabin crew dispute.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA moves to quell cabin crew dispute.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Thursday it had sent a proposal to arbitration service ACAS to try to settle its dispute with cabin crew as a strike deadline loomed.

The airline's stewards and stewardesses have threatened a three-day strike next week over plans to restructure pay and conditions, which are part of its goal of saving one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) by the end of the century.
Officials from the Transport & General Workers Unions say the package would cut cabin crew salaries and have bristled at BA sealing a deal with the smaller Cabin Crew 89 union.

A BA spokesman said the airline's proposal addressed two main concerns -- the union's fears about its members being worse off under the new arrangement, and the relationships between the two cabin crew unions.

"We hope that the proposals will be acceptable. This provides a way forward and we hope the unions will take this chance to sit down with us...We will await a response from ACAS and the TGWU and in the meantime it's business as usual," the spokesman said.
The T&G union, which represents most of the 9,000-strong mainline ground crew, said it was aware of the proposal but declined further comment.
On Tuesday, BA offered arbitrated talks in an attempt to break the five-month deadlock and avert strikes which will hit the carrier in the busy -- and profitable -- summer season.

BA also faces trouble on the ground, where staff voted last week for strike action to protest the sale of the catering unit at London's Heathrow airport, part of BA's drive to outsource more non-core services.
The spokesman said direct talks had started earlier this week and were continuing on Thursday. He declined to comment on their status.
BA faced more bad news this week after Britain failed to settle disagreements with the European Union over BA's proposed alliance with American Airlines.

The industrial disputes, the first since the new Labour government was elected, have been marked by acrimony. BA chief executive Bob Ayling has accused unions of reverting to militant '1970s style trade unionism'.
Staff representatives have accused BA of intimidation as the carrier threatened to sack striking workers and curb benefits while training senior staff to fill in emergency slots.
BA shares were little moved by news of the proposal, trading five pence higher at 696p at midday in London.
